'''Sir John Wilson''' (6 August 1741, [[Applethwaite]], [[Westmorland]] &ndash; 18 October 1793, [[Kendal]], Westmorland)<ref>[{{Google books|plainurl=y|id=OVkoCcszEZ0C|page=50|text=1741–1793}} Robinson (2003), p. 50].</ref> was an [[England|English]] mathematician and judge.  [[Wilson's theorem]] is named after him.

Wilson attended school in [[Staveley, Cumbria]] before going up to [[Peterhouse, Cambridge|Peterhouse]], [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] in 1757,<ref name=Venn>{{acad|id=WL757J|name=Wilson, John}}</ref> where he was a student of  [[Edward Waring]].  He was [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Senior Wrangler]] in 1761.<ref name=Venn /> He was later knighted, and became a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1782.  He was [[Court of Common Pleas (England)|Judge of Common Pleas]] from 1786 until his death in 1793.
